Attendees: Chris Miller (Redwood AE), Priya Rao (Redwood SE), Liam Nguyen (Redwood SE), Maya Patel (Nimbus CTO), Javier Costa (Nimbus Lead ML), Sarah Lee (Nimbus Infra)

summary: Deep technical session on p95/p99 tail latency causes and mitigation: KV cache hit rates, batching strategies, streaming vs non-streaming tradeoffs, quantization impact, network hops in VPC/on-prem, and recommended experiments for Nimbus to run in pilot. topics: p95 vs p99 tail latency analysis
VPC/on-prem network hops and TCP/TLS overhead

transcript:
[00:00] Chris Miller: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. we wanna deep dive on p95 and p99 tail numbers you sent, thanks for sending the traces. quick intros?
[00:12] Maya Patel: I m Maya, CTO at Nimbus. we re trying to get our assistant into the robots for the next launch. Latency is our big blocker.
[00:18] Chris Miller: cool, Javier?
[00:20] Javier Costa: Javier, ML lead. Our main constraints: interactive prompts, seq len usually 128-512, some longer op logs up to 1k, target p95 under 200ms and p99 under 400ms for hosted flows. For on-robot (private) we want p95 under 120ms.
[00:34] Priya Rao: thanks. Quick caveat — transcript had some words swapped from our internal notes, so if anything is off call it out.
[00:40] Sarah Lee: I'm Sarah, infra. we have both cloud-hosted and on-prem nodes; networking and firewall policies are strict.
[00:47] Chris Miller: Great. So we looked at the traces you sent. Summary: p50 is fine (~60ms), p95 around 220ms, p99 spikes to 1.1s in some windows. A few things jumped out: KV cache hit rate low on some workloads, spikes align with cold KV cache miss + large batch formation, and a couple of network async hops — looks like cross-az calls.
[01:12] Javier Costa: Can you explain the KV cache behavior a bit? we thought our prefix caching would cover most interactions.
[01:18] Priya Rao: Sure. Redwood's KV cache stores key/value activations per request prefix; hit rate depends on prefix similarity and cache TTL and also on whether requests are pinned to the same replica. If requests route across different replicas or if you have different seq len distributions, cache hits drop. In your traces we saw hot-path requests that hashed to different pods causing frequent misses.
[01:36] Maya Patel: so is that routing? we use round robin LB in our private VPC.
[01:41] Priya Rao: round robin can be fine for throughput but it reduces cache locality. For low tail latency you want sticky routing at least for a short TTL, or use consistent hashing by client / conversation id so the same conversation hits the same replica and benefits from KV cache.
[01:55] Chris Miller: also worth noting that continuous batching can exacerbate p99 if head-of-line requests wait for batch fill. You saw spikes where a request waited 200-300ms while waiting to reach batch window.
[02:06] Javier Costa: our batching is auto at 50ms or 8 items, whichever first. is that too aggressive?
[02:12] Priya Rao: It depends. For interactive low-latency targets, smaller max batch sizes and tighter max delay helps; but that raises GPU utilization and cost. There's a sweet spot: smaller steady-state batch target with overflow burst capacity. We recommend dynamic batching policy: target 4-8 tokens per batch for short seq lengths, with preemptive flush if head-of-line latency exceeds threshold. We'll share example configs.
[02:31] Liam Nguyen: Another vector: streaming vs non-streaming. token-by-token streaming adds per-token overhead if your stack does synchronous network crossings per token. If you can stream over a persistent gRPC or websocket with HTTP/2 and keep-alive, per-token overhead is low. But if you use many short HTTP requests or serialize each token, p99 explodes.
[02:50] Sarah Lee: We currently proxy through an internal API gateway that does TLS termination and some auth introspection on each request — that might add a network hop per token.
[02:58] Priya Rao: That's a common anti-pattern. For streaming, you want to preserve a single long-lived connection per client, run auth once on connect and pass auth token in the channel, and avoid per-token routing through gateways.
[03:10] Maya Patel: What about quantization? we wanted to try int8 to save cost — will that help latency or hurt p99?
[03:16] Priya Rao: Quantization generally reduces per-token compute time and memory bandwidth, often improving throughput and median latency. But sometimes quantized kernels have higher variance on some GPUs depending on kernel paths and sequence length. For p99 you need to test: int8 typically helps but watch for occasional kernel fallback or dequant/deq overheads. We recommend running per-model microbenchmarks with your seq-length distribution.
[03:35] Chris Miller: Also watch KV cache interplay — quantization plus caching can change memory footprint and cache eviction patterns on the GPU, so combined effects matter.
[03:43] Javier Costa: We saw a few 1s spikes that line up with cross-az traffic — can you talk network hops?
[03:49] Priya Rao: Sure. Network hops matter. If traffic crosses AZ or exits a VPC to a private control plane, each hop adds ~1-5ms for intra-cloud, more for on-prem to cloud. But worse is packetization and TLS handshake costs if a connection is new. For a p99 target, you want: TCP keep-alive, reused TLS sessions, minimum cross-az calls, and ideally colocate model serving in same AZ/subnet as the gateway. Also, MTU mismatches and NAT gateways can add jitter.
[04:16] Sarah Lee: Our on-prem nodes are in a colo with a firewall and strict NAT — is there guidance for reducing jitter?
[04:21] Priya Rao: Use local load balancer inside the colo, terminate TLS at the edge of the private cluster, and avoid hairpinning through corporate firewalls for the dataplane. If you can run Redwood Private inside the same network, we can do an air-gapped deployment where control plane is separate from dataplane to avoid extra hops.
[04:39] Maya Patel: You mentioned warm start and cold start; how much does model load factor into p99?
[04:44] Chris Miller: Model load is huge if your workload triggers scale-out or cold container start mid-traffic. Cold starts can be multiple seconds. Mitigations: keep a pool of warm replicas, use fast model loading (quantized checkpoints), prewarm on deploy, and use a staged rollout so traffic doesn't hit scaling boundaries unexpectedly.
[05:00] Javier Costa: about the batching backpressure — can the runtime preempt a batch if a high-priority low-latency request arrives?
[05:06] Priya Rao: Yes, Redwood supports prioritization and preemptive flush: you can mark certain requests as low-latency-critical which go to a 'fast lane' with smaller batch sizes. There's also adaptive batching where the runtime watches latency SLOs and tightens batch windows under tail pressure.
[05:20] Liam Nguyen: Another trick: prefix caching to reduce tokens per call. If the system can compress common prompt parts via cached KV entries, you reduce compute. But this only works if routing and cache locality are good.
[05:31] Sarah Lee: Is there a recommended metric set we should forward for debugging?
[05:35] Priya Rao: Yes — per-request: enqueue_time, batch_wait_ms, kv_cache_hit, model_infer_ms, kernel_ms, gpu_load, rdma_stats (if using RDMA), network_hop_count, tls_handshake_count, connection_age. Also per-replica CPU/GPU temperature and memory evictions.
[05:51] Chris Miller: We add logs linking request IDs end-to-end so you can trace where time is spent across proxies. That helped pinpoint a config bug for another customer.
[05:59] Javier Costa: For streaming flows — we have device-level constraints where we can't open too many persistent connections. Does Redwood support multiplexing many sessions over fewer channels?
[06:07] Priya Rao: Yes, you can multiplex conversations over fewer persistent channels using a session-level protocol. That reduces TLS memory and connection churn. It does require your client to implement a small session manager. We can share a sample client.
[06:19] Maya Patel: Any quick wins we should attempt during pilot?
[06:22] Priya Rao: Three quick wins: 1) enable sticky routing by conversation id for 24-48h and check KV cache hit rate delta; 2) reduce max batch delay to 20ms for low-latency lane; 3) run int8 microbenchmarks on a staging replica to compare p99.
[06:36] Chris Miller: we'll also send a sample benchmark harness and a data sheet showing expected median and tail under different configs.
[06:41] Sarah Lee: About security for private deployments do you require egress for the control plane?
[06:45] Chris Miller: For Redwood Private we offer an option where the control plane can be managed-while-keeping dataplane fully isolated. You can use an air-gapped deployment or limited egress for telemetry; we support customer KMS/HSM and local audit logs. We'll share the SOC2 pack.
[06:58] Javier Costa: What about quantization fallbacks you mentioned — how do we detect kernel fallback issues?
[07:03] Priya Rao: Runtime exposes kernel path metrics; look for operations that take much longer on int8 than fp16 for certain seq lengths. Also watch for increased GPU memory thrash and additional memcpy metrics. We can help interpret kernel traces.
[07:16] Maya Patel: On cost tradeoffs — reducing p99 usually increases cost due to warm replicas and smaller batches; any heuristics?
[07:22] Chris Miller: Right. Heuristics: isolate low-latency-critical traffic into a smaller fleet (dedicated capacity) and keep bulk workloads on cheaper shared capacity. Use autoscaling with fast warm pools and burst capacity. Redwood Optimize can recommend quantization + batch combos for your workload to hit cost targets.
[07:38] Sarah Lee: For the pilot, how long to see meaningful p99 changes?
[07:41] Priya Rao: Often within 48-72 hours of running with sticky routing + adjusted batching you see KV cache hit improvements and tail reductions. Quantization plus kernel tuning may take a week.
[07:52] Chris Miller: Let's recap open items and next steps.
[07:55] Maya Patel: before that, a quick question: we use edge devices with intermittent connectivity. Any tolerance?
[08:00] Priya Rao: For intermittent connections we recommend an on-device fallback lightweight model for short responses and sync to cluster for heavy ops. For p99 on connected flows, ensure session reconnection preserves cache affinity by mapping device ID to consistent hash.
[08:14] Chris Miller: Ok recap — Priya sends KV-cache and batching runbook and sample configs; Chris sends Dedicated pricing and SOC2/security docs; Nimbus shares traces and network topology; schedule pilot week of Dec 13. Any other asks?
[08:30] Javier Costa: Please include a sample client for multiplexing.
[08:33] Priya Rao: Will do.
[08:35] Chris Miller: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email with links.
[08:40] Maya Patel: thanks all.
[08:41] End of recording.

Notes on transcript quality: occasional mis-transcriptions (e.g., "K V cache" split, product names). Speaker labels are accurate but there were a few cross-talks that the auto-transcript merged.
